title: Ionic, covalent, hydrogen and metallic bonding
blurb: Predict the bond type from the elements involved, tell polar from nonpolar sharing and explain what hydrogen bonds do for water and DNA.
question: Sodium chloride melts at a very high temperature and conducts electricity once dissolved, yet water, a much lighter molecule, still has a surprisingly high boiling point. Which kinds of bonding explain each fact?

teach.body: Formally, a chemical bond is an attraction that holds atoms together, formed when atoms transfer or share valence electrons to reach a stable arrangement (usually an octet). In plain English: atoms bond to fill their outer shell. Whether they hand electrons over or share them depends on how hard each atom pulls on electrons, its electronegativity. A big difference means transfer; a small one means sharing.

teach.caption: Ionic bonds form when the electronegativity difference is large (roughly above 1.7 to 2.0).

steps.label: Cl: 2, 8, 7
steps.sub: One electron short of an octet

teach.caption: As a solid, the ions are locked in place, so it does not conduct. Melt or dissolve it and the ions move freely, so it conducts.

teach.body: In a covalent bond, atoms share electron pairs. If both atoms pull equally, the sharing is nonpolar: H₂, O₂, Cl₂ and C–H bonds. If one atom pulls harder, the sharing is polar and creates partial charges: H₂O, NH₃, HCl. Water is bent, with a partial negative oxygen and partial positive hydrogens, so the whole molecule is polar. Sharing one, two or three pairs gives single, double or triple bonds.

teach.body: A hydrogen bond is a weak attraction BETWEEN molecules: a hydrogen atom bonded to N, O or F is drawn to a lone pair on another N, O or F. It is not a bond inside a molecule and is much weaker than ionic or covalent bonds. Hydrogen bonds link water molecules (high boiling point, surface tension), hold DNA base pairs together and shape protein secondary structure.

teach.caption: All three intermolecular forces are weaker than ionic or covalent bonds.

teach.h: Scenario: Tasha explains saline and water
teach.body: Tasha, a nursing applicant, is asked why normal saline conducts electricity. NaCl forms from a metal (sodium) and a nonmetal (chlorine), so it is ionic; in water the ions separate and carry current. Next: why does water boil at 100 °C when similar small molecules are gases? Water is polar, and hydrogen bonds between its molecules must be overcome before it can boil.

teach.text: Ionic = TRANSFER, covalent = SHARING (the reverse is the classic slip). Ionic bonds need a metal plus a nonmetal, not two nonmetals. Hydrogen bonds are the WEAKEST of these bond types, not the strongest, and they form between molecules, not inside them.

items: Ionic: electrons transferred, metal + nonmetal, lattice, high melting point, conducts when melted or dissolved.
Covalent: electrons shared between nonmetals; polar if unequal (H₂O, NH₃, HCl), nonpolar if equal (H₂, O₂).
Metallic: cations in a sea of delocalized electrons, so metals conduct and are malleable.
Hydrogen bonds: weak attractions between molecules (H on N, O or F); in water, DNA and proteins.
London < dipole-dipole < hydrogen bonds, all weaker than ionic or covalent bonds.

summary: You can now predict whether atoms will form ionic, covalent or metallic bonds, tell polar from nonpolar covalent bonds and link each bond type to its properties. You can also explain hydrogen bonding and rank intermolecular forces by strength.

A.q: Which pair of elements is most likely to form an ionic bond?
options: Carbon and oxygen
Nitrogen and hydrogen
Magnesium and oxygen
Chlorine and chlorine
A.why: Magnesium is a metal and oxygen a nonmetal; the large electronegativity difference leads to electron transfer (MgO).

whyNot.0: Carbon and oxygen are both nonmetals, so they share electrons (covalent, as in CO₂).
whyNot.1: Nitrogen and hydrogen are nonmetals; NH₃ has polar covalent bonds.
whyNot.3: Two identical chlorine atoms pull equally, forming a nonpolar covalent bond (Cl₂).

A.q: In a covalent bond, the atoms:
options: share pairs of electrons
transfer electrons fully
share a sea of electrons
exchange protons between nuclei
A.why: Covalent bonds form when nonmetal atoms share one or more pairs of electrons.

whyNot.1: Complete transfer of electrons describes an ionic bond.
whyNot.2: A sea of delocalized electrons describes metallic bonding.
whyNot.3: Protons stay in the nucleus; bonding involves only valence electrons.

A.q: A hydrogen bond forms between a hydrogen atom bonded to N, O or F and:
options: a hydrogen atom in a nearby molecule
a lone pair on a nearby N, O or F atom
a carbon atom within the same molecule
a metal cation in the same solution
A.why: The partially positive hydrogen is attracted to a lone pair on an electronegative N, O or F atom of another molecule.

whyNot.0: Two partially positive hydrogens would repel, not attract.
whyNot.2: Hydrogen bonds act between molecules, and carbon is not one of the electronegative partners.
whyNot.3: Attractions to metal cations are ion interactions, not hydrogen bonds.

B.q: Solid sodium chloride does not conduct electricity, but molten sodium chloride does. Why?
options: Melting turns it into a covalent compound
Melting frees electrons from the nuclei
Solid NaCl contains no charged particles
Melting lets the ions move freely
B.why: Ionic solids hold their ions fixed in a lattice. Once melted (or dissolved), the ions can move and carry current.

whyNot.0: Melting is a physical change; NaCl stays ionic.
whyNot.1: Ionic compounds conduct through moving ions, not free electrons as metals do.
whyNot.2: Solid NaCl is made entirely of charged ions; they are just locked in place.

B.q: Which molecule contains polar covalent bonds?
options: H₂
NH₃
Cl₂
CH₄
B.why: Nitrogen pulls harder on shared electrons than hydrogen, so the N–H bonds in ammonia are polar.

whyNot.0: Two identical hydrogen atoms share equally: nonpolar.
whyNot.2: Identical chlorine atoms share equally: nonpolar.
whyNot.3: C–H bonds are treated as nonpolar: carbon and hydrogen pull on shared electrons almost equally.

B.q: Which type of bonding explains why metals are malleable and conduct electricity?
options: Ionic bonding
Hydrogen bonding
Metallic bonding
Polar covalent bonding
B.why: In metallic bonding, cations sit in a sea of delocalized electrons that carry current and let layers slide without breaking.

whyNot.0: Ionic solids are brittle and do not conduct as solids.
whyNot.1: Hydrogen bonds are weak attractions between molecules, not bonds within a metal.
whyNot.3: Polar covalent bonds are between nonmetals and do not provide free electrons.

C.q: Water has a much higher boiling point than other molecules of similar size. Which explains this?
options: Hydrogen bonds between water molecules
Ionic bonds between H and O atoms
Covalent bonds breaking as water boils
Metallic bonds among the oxygen atoms
C.why: Polar water molecules are linked by hydrogen bonds, which take extra energy to overcome before water can boil.

whyNot.1: Hydrogen and oxygen are both nonmetals; their bonds within water are polar covalent, not ionic.
whyNot.2: Boiling is physical: it separates molecules and does not break the covalent bonds inside them.
whyNot.3: Oxygen is a nonmetal; metallic bonding occurs only among metal atoms.

C.q: Which statement correctly compares bond and force strengths?
options: Hydrogen bonds are stronger than covalent bonds
Ionic bonds form between two nonmetal atoms
A single bond is stronger than a triple bond
Dipole-dipole forces are weaker than H bonds
C.why: Intermolecular forces rank London dispersion < dipole-dipole < hydrogen bonds.

whyNot.0: Hydrogen bonds are much weaker than covalent or ionic bonds.
whyNot.1: Ionic bonds form between a metal and a nonmetal.
whyNot.2: Strength rises from single to double to triple bonds.

C.q: Element X is a group 1 metal and element Y is a group 17 nonmetal. The compound they form is most likely:
options: covalent, formed by sharing electrons
ionic, with a high melting point
metallic, with a sea of electrons
nonpolar, with equal electron sharing
C.why: A group 1 metal loses one electron and a halogen gains one: a metal plus nonmetal transfer forms an ionic lattice with a high melting point.

whyNot.0: Sharing occurs between nonmetals; X is a metal with a very different electronegativity from Y.
whyNot.2: Metallic bonding needs metal atoms only; Y is a nonmetal.
whyNot.3: Equal sharing needs similar electronegativities; group 1 and group 17 differ greatly.

reteach.title: Playground rules for electrons
reteach.question: Picture kids on a playground with balls and jump ropes. How do giving, sharing and pooling toys match the bond types?

blocks.body: Ionic: one kid simply gives a ball to another. Now one is 'down a ball' (positive) and one is 'up a ball' (negative), and they stick together by attraction. Covalent: two kids hold one jump rope together; if one is stronger, the rope drifts toward them (polar). Metallic: the whole class tosses a shared pile of balls around (a sea of electrons). Hydrogen bonds: quick high-fives between kids in different groups, real but easily broken.

blocks.h: Match the playground to the bond
head: Playground
Bond
Example

blocks.text: Giving away is ionic; sharing is covalent. If you catch yourself saying 'ionic bonds share electrons', flip it.

explain.body: A metal transfers electrons to a nonmetal. The resulting cation and anion attract, forming a crystal lattice: high melting point, brittle, conducts when melted or dissolved.

test.q: When sodium and chlorine form sodium chloride, what happens?
options: Na gains an electron from Cl
Na and Cl share an electron pair
Na gives an electron to Cl
Cl gives a proton to Na
test.why: Sodium (2, 8, 1) loses its single valence electron to chlorine (2, 8, 7), forming Na⁺ and Cl⁻.

whyNot.0: The direction is reversed: metals lose electrons; chlorine is the one that gains.
whyNot.1: Sharing describes covalent bonding between nonmetals; Na is a metal.
whyNot.3: Protons never move between atoms in chemical bonding.

explain.body: Nonmetals share electron pairs. Equal pull gives nonpolar bonds (H₂, O₂, Cl₂); unequal pull gives polar bonds with partial charges (H₂O, NH₃, HCl). Water is bent and polar.

test.q: Why is a water molecule polar?
options: O pulls shared electrons more than H
H and O share their electrons equally
Water is held together by ionic bonds
Water has a straight, linear shape
test.why: Oxygen is more electronegative, so shared electrons sit closer to it; with water's bent shape, the molecule has a partial negative end and a partial positive end.

whyNot.1: Equal sharing would make the bonds nonpolar.
whyNot.2: Water's bonds are polar covalent: H and O are both nonmetals.
whyNot.3: Water is bent, not linear; that bend is part of why the molecule is polar.

explain.body: Metal atoms release valence electrons into a shared, delocalized 'sea' around the cations. The mobile electrons conduct heat and electricity, and the layers can slide, making metals malleable and ductile.

test.q: Metallic bonding is best described as:
options: a transfer of electrons from metal to nonmetal
a shared pair between two nonmetal atoms
an attraction between polar molecules
metal cations in a sea of free electrons
test.why: Metallic bonding is the attraction between metal cations and the delocalized electrons around them.

whyNot.0: Electron transfer from metal to nonmetal is ionic bonding.
whyNot.1: A shared pair between nonmetals is a covalent bond.
whyNot.2: Attractions between polar molecules are dipole-dipole forces.

explain.body: A weak attraction between molecules: H bonded to N, O or F is drawn to a lone pair on another N, O or F. They give water its high boiling point and surface tension and hold DNA base pairs together.

test.q: Which structures are held together partly by hydrogen bonds?
options: Table salt crystals
Paired DNA bases
Copper wire
Methane molecules
test.why: Complementary DNA bases pair through hydrogen bonds between N–H and O or N atoms.

whyNot.0: Salt crystals are held by ionic bonds between Na⁺ and Cl⁻.
whyNot.2: Copper is held by metallic bonding.
whyNot.3: Methane's C–H bonds are nonpolar covalent; H bonded to carbon cannot form hydrogen bonds.
